problems.1: Wholesale forecasts are far off and overconfident
problems.2: Machinery's entities do not add up to the official totals
problems.3: New orders are not determined by data
problems.4: The estimation is unsettled in Retail and for several individual quantities
problems.5: Capacity forecasts are overconfident, while capacity growth is poorly learned
problems.6: The uncertainty ranges are miscalibrated in both directions
problems.7: Ranges around sector totals are too tight against official statistics
problems.8: Inventories are set mostly by assumption and fit observations poorly
problems.9: Order flow in service sectors comes from the model, not from data
problems.10: Some parameters lean on priors, and the 91% figure may flatter
problems.11: Forecast error is mostly present already at the current month

fixes.fix: Give Wholesale an official price statistic, such as a monthly price index for wholesale trade. Wholesale has no price observations and no official statistic, and on an earlier synthetic world its price and unit cost drifted 10-12% off by the later run dates, which a later re-estimate then corrects. Pinning the price level would also pin the volume that the revenue observations imply.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the price statistic and rerun Wholesale at all four run dates on two seeds; Wholesale's gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 12.4% and its hit rate rise toward 90/100.

fixes.fix: Fit Wholesale three times with different random numbers and pool the simulated copies from all three fits into one forecast. On an earlier world, Wholesale's accuracy changed a lot from one set of random numbers to the next (average error from 5% to 14%), so one fit can land far from the next year's fit. Pooling makes the forecast range admit that uncertainty and steadies its middle line.
fixes.test: Run Wholesale at four run dates with three fits pooled per date; its hit rate on Forecasts against later estimates should move from 76/100 toward 90/100 and its gap should shrink.

fixes.fix: Estimate one capacity growth rate for all Wholesale entities instead of one per entity, since only 14% of the entity growth rates are learned from data. This was tried once before Wholesale got its inventory statistic and a longer search, and it did not clearly help (one of two fits on target, and the shared rate was no better pinned). This time it would be tested with both in place.
fixes.test: Rerun Wholesale at four run dates on two seeds with a shared growth rate; Wholesale's gap and hit rate on Forecasts against later estimates should improve.

fixes.fix: During fitting, anchor the overall size of Machinery's representative entities to the official production statistic, as 11 other sectors already do, since a steady 5.8% gap points to the size of the untracked firms. On an earlier world this hurt Machinery (error 5.6% to 7.9%), but that was before a fix to dollar-valued order-book observations, which matters because Machinery is measured in dollars.
fixes.test: Rerun Machinery at four run dates on two seeds with the anchor; on Sector totals against official statistics, Machinery production should move from 0/100 toward 90/100 with a gap under 2%.

fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust Machinery's order level and overdue orders directly, as it already does for Semiconductors, so the sector-wide unfilled-orders statistic can correct the order book month by month. In Semiconductors this ended runaway order books, and their results were mild in five of five backtests. Machinery shows the same signs: it misses too many observations and its new orders become less certain when data are added.
fixes.test: Rerun Machinery at four run dates on two seeds; Observations against the model should move from 85/100 toward 90/100, and the official production and utilization statistics should agree more often.

fixes.fix: Give Machinery a longer, full-strength search for its parameters (more steps per round, more rounds, more patience before stopping), as Oil and gas and Wholesale already have. On earlier worlds the true parameters scored better than Machinery's fit, so the search stops short. A stronger search alone did not close that gap before, however, which is why the odds are modest.
fixes.test: Rerun Machinery at four run dates on two seeds with the longer search; the official production hit rate and the observation hit rate should both rise.

fixes.fix: Check the conversion between Machinery's dollar volume and the official production index and utilization rate, step by step, against the input bundle. The evaluator suspected a unit error, and dollar-valued quantities in this world were recently changed. A synthetic world builds its statistics with the model's own conversion, so an error is unlikely, but the check is cheap.
fixes.test: Recompute Machinery's production and utilization totals from one run's output by hand and compare them with the official series; a scale error would show as a constant gap close to 5.8%.

fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust each entity's order level in the sectors where new orders become less certain with data (Housing, Retail, Data centers, Machinery, Airlines), as it already does in Semiconductors. Today the order level is a fixed parameter, so observations of the order book, shipments and occupancy can only move orders through monthly surprises, which push the copies apart. With the level adjustable, the same observations can narrow it.
fixes.test: Rerun those five sectors at four run dates on two seeds; their new-orders spread ratios on What the data pin down should fall below 1.

fixes.fix: Add official statistics that measure new orders directly: manufacturers' new orders for Machinery and Semiconductors, new home sales for Housing, and newly signed leases for Data centers. Today no observation measures new orders, so they are inferred from the order book and shipments. Measuring them directly would pin them.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new statistics and run a full four-date backtest; new-orders spread ratios on What the data pin down should drop below 0.8 in those sectors.

fixes.fix: Measure each entity's order response to demand against the entity's own average demand over the window, so the order level and that response stop trading off. Past diagnosis found the two on a ridge where orders fit about equally well while the states come out wrong. This firms up the estimates but may not change how the filter spreads the copies.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; the new-orders spread ratios and the share of order parameters learned from data on What the data pin down should both improve.

fixes.fix: Compute the spread ratio from total spread over the history with and without data, rather than averaging month-by-month ratios, and report months where single copies ran away. Averaging lets a few months in which copies barely disagree without data produce very large values, so if that is the cause the ratios will shrink, and if not, the measure shows where the problem lies.
fixes.test: Refilter the existing fits at all four run dates with the new measure; Retail's ratios of 3.2-3.6 and the other values above 1.2 on What the data pin down should fall toward or below 1, or the runaway months should be identified.

fixes.fix: Pull every simulated copy toward the official statistic's central value, treating its uncertainty as noise, instead of pulling each copy toward a different draw from the input bundle. The current way adds the bundle's own spread to the copies. Where that spread exceeds the model's, data make the copies disagree more.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; the spread ratios above 1.2 in Retail, Housing, Hospitals and Hotels should fall below 1, without lowering the hit rates on Sector totals against official statistics.

fixes.fix: Replace the filter's random perturbation of observations with a deterministic version of the same update, which can only narrow the copies' spread. With 100 copies and many observations, the random noise added today can widen quantities the observations barely bear on. This is a larger change to the filter, affecting every sector.
fixes.test: Run full four-date backtests on two seeds; no spread ratio on What the data pin down should exceed 1.2, and forecast gaps should not get worse.

fixes.fix: Limit what each sector-wide observation can move: let it update only the quantities it measures and their direct inputs, not every hidden quantity in every entity of the sector. With 100 copies, chance correlations between a sector total and unrelated quantities, such as one entity's lost demand, are large enough to push copies apart.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; the unsettled ratios (Retail, Hospitals' lost demand, Housing's new orders, Oil and gas overdue orders) should fall below 1.2.

fixes.fix: Add a small monthly capacity revision to every kind of business, as pipeline producers already have, so that capacity can drift away from its planned path. In forecasts the copies would then spread out further ahead, and stated-capacity observations could correct the level. Today capacity can change only through its fitted growth rate, so the range stays as narrow as today's well-known level.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; Capacity on Forecasts against later estimates should move from 74/100 toward 90/100 without a larger gap.

fixes.fix: Widen the forecast range for capacity on its own, with a factor set so that the range holds the next run's estimate about 90% of the time on earlier synthetic worlds. Today one widening factor serves every quantity, and capacity, which the data pin down well at each run, ends up too narrow for how much the level moves between runs.
fixes.test: Refilter existing runs of earlier worlds to set the factor, then rescore this world; Capacity's hit rate on Forecasts against later estimates should be near 90/100.

fixes.fix: Estimate one capacity growth rate per sector in the sectors where entity growth rates are poorly learned (Autos, Retail, Wholesale, Hotels, Housing), choosing sector by sector by how well each choice predicts withheld observations. One growth rate per sector is better pinned, which should make capacity forecasts move less between runs. In a past Wholesale test, though, the shared rate was no better pinned than the separate ones.
fixes.test: Run withheld-observation checks for those five sectors at two run dates, then a four-date run of the chosen sectors; capacity growth's share learned from data and Capacity's hit rate should rise.

fixes.fix: Replace the single widening factor for all ranges with one factor per quantity and forecast horizon, set on several earlier synthetic worlds where the truth is known. Today every quantity is widened by the same amount (about 1.9 times for forecasts), set on an older world before several model changes. Quantities the data pin down need less widening than quantities that come mostly from the model.
fixes.test: Refilter and rescore existing runs of earlier worlds to set the factors, then rescore this world; on Forecasts against later estimates most quantities should land between 85/100 and 95/100 instead of 74-100/100.

fixes.fix: Mark quantities whose spread ratio is 0.8 or above on Forecasts against later estimates, and leave them out of the overall hit rate. For these the later estimate also comes from the model's equations, so the check compares the model with itself, which is why input inventory and lead time score 100/100. The overall figure would then describe only quantities the data inform.
fixes.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; the overall hit rate should describe only data-informed quantities, and the 100/100 rows should be marked as checked against the model itself.

fixes.fix: Make the simulated copies carry the uncertainty that widening stands in for, by drawing sector parameters and group averages from wider ranges where the data leave them loose, then reducing the widening factor. Ranges would then be wide only where parameters are uncertain. Earlier attempts to add parameter uncertainty raised hit rates only partly, so some widening would remain.
fixes.test: Run full four-date backtests on two seeds with the factors recalibrated; the spread of hit rates across quantities on Forecasts against later estimates should narrow.

fixes.fix: When checking sector totals against official statistics, include the statistic's own uncertainty, the amount the filter already assumes when it pulls totals toward it. Today the range is only the spread between the model's copies and the statistic's draws. Because the filter pulls each copy toward its own draw, that spread is very small, and gaps under 1% count as misses.
fixes.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; Hotels and Hospitals employees and Chemicals and Food utilization should move toward 90/100, while Machinery production (5.8% off) should still disagree.

fixes.fix: Stop using the same official statistic twice: once to set the size of the representative entities during fitting, and again when the filter pulls sector totals toward it. Counting the same information twice makes the model too sure of those totals. All five series with ranges that are too tight are in sectors that use both.
fixes.test: Rerun Hotels, Hospitals, Chemicals and Food at four run dates on two seeds with the official statistic used only once; their hit rates on Sector totals against official statistics should rise toward 90/100 with gaps no larger.

fixes.fix: Let labor per unit of output drift slowly over time within each sector, instead of holding it fixed. Employment is now a fixed multiple of output, so its range is only as wide as output's and leaves out changes in productivity. A drifting ratio would give employment a range of its own.
fixes.test: Rerun Hotels and Hospitals at four run dates on two seeds; their employee hit rates on Sector totals against official statistics should rise from 51/100 and 63/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.fix: Add observations of input inventory, such as official materials inventories for manufacturers and companies' reported raw materials. No observation measures input inventory today, which is why its spread ratio is near 1 in all eight sectors that have it. Without data, nothing else in the model can pin it.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with these observations and run a full four-date backtest; input inventory's spread ratios on What the data pin down should drop below 0.8.

fixes.fix: Remove the filter rule that stops adjusting a simulated copy's finished stock for good once that copy has run out of stock with orders late. A past investigation found this rule but never tested removing it. A copy that runs out early in the window can then never be brought back to the stock that firms report, which fits the finished-inventory observations missing too often.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; finished inventory on Observations against the model should move from 84/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.fix: Give each entity its own normal stock level, pooled toward the sector's, instead of one level for the whole sector. The filter keeps pulling every firm's stock back toward the sector's normal level, so firms that hold persistently more or less stock than that drift away from their own reports. In an earlier world, one sector's stock observations were not followed for this reason.
fixes.test: Run a full four-date backtest; finished inventory on Observations against the model should approach 90/100, and its spread ratios should fall below 0.8.

fixes.fix: Add official sector-wide finished-goods inventories for the manufacturing sectors (Food, Autos, Chemicals, Steel), as already exists for Oil and gas and Wholesale. Most of a sector's stock belongs to representative entities, and no observation reaches them. In Wholesale such a statistic brought the sector to target, while in Oil and gas it first did harm until a related fix.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with these statistics and run a full four-date backtest; finished inventory's spread ratios should fall well below 0.8 in those sectors and its observation hit rate should rise.

fixes.fix: Show quantities that never vary among the simulated copies (Data centers' overdue orders, phantom orders and lead time) as fixed by the model's structure instead of with a spread ratio of 1.00. When a quantity has no spread with or without data, the measure falls back to exactly 1. That reads as "comes from assumptions" when the quantity is simply constant for this kind of business.
fixes.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; Data centers' overdue orders, phantom orders and lead time should show as fixed by structure rather than 1.00.

fixes.fix: Let the filter adjust the order level of Hotels, Hospitals and Data centers directly, so that occupancy, load-factor and staffed-bed observations can move demand rather than only output. Today a reading that shows a fuller hotel can change little in the order side. This is the same change that steadied Semiconductors' order book.
fixes.test: Rerun those three sectors at four run dates on two seeds; their shipments, order book and lead time spread ratios should fall below 0.8.

fixes.fix: Add observations of advance bookings: rooms and seats already booked for coming months for Hotels and Airlines, and leases signed but not yet started for Data centers, where that observation is still sparse. These measure the order book in service businesses directly.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with booking observations and run a full four-date backtest; order book and lead time spread ratios in Hotels and Data centers should drop below 0.8.

fixes.fix: Move the parameters that data rarely pin for each entity (emissions slope, capacity growth, list-price gap) to one value per sector, chosen sector by sector by how well each choice predicts withheld observations. Past tests found that sharing parameters helped Food, helped Machinery only when the starting guess was close, and hurt Steel. The choice has to be made per sector, not everywhere.
fixes.test: Run withheld-observation checks at two run dates in the sectors with the weakest parameters, then a four-date run with the chosen settings; the share of parameters learned from data should rise without worse forecast gaps.

fixes.fix: Measure how much each parameter is learned by comparing its uncertainty after fitting with its uncertainty given only the group's average, not the starting guess. Today the pull toward the group average counts as learning, so the 91% figure can flatter weakly observed entities. The figure will probably fall, but it will then show where the data truly shape the estimates.
fixes.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; What the data pin down should report both the current and the stricter figure for every sector.

fixes.fix: Add observations that bear on the weakest parameters: earlier price observations for each entity (starting markup), more list-price observations alongside transaction prices (list-price gap), and emissions reported over a wider range of utilization (emissions slope). Pooling cannot replace data for parameters that few observations touch.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the added observations and run a full four-date backtest; the shares of starting markup, list-price gap and emissions slope learned from data should rise.

fixes.fix: Start each run's fit from the previous run's estimates instead of from the starting guesses. Fits from the same data vary from one set of random numbers to the next, so independent fits a year apart disagree about the present even where the data barely changed. Starting from last year's answer should keep re-estimates closer, unless that answer was wrong.
fixes.test: Run a four-date backtest with the dates in sequence, each starting from the last; the current-month gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall below 2.1%.

fixes.fix: Combine three fits per run, each with different random numbers, into one forecast. This averages out the luck of a single fit, which on earlier worlds moved a sector's error severalfold, so the present should be revised less when a later run refits.
fixes.test: Run a four-date backtest with three fits per sector and date; the current-month gap should fall below 2.1% and the gap should grow more steeply with the forecast horizon.

fixes.fix: Run the filter with 200 simulated copies instead of 100 to reduce the chance part of each run's middle line. Past checks of the same fits with different filter random numbers found the filter's own randomness to be a modest part of the error.
fixes.test: Refilter the existing fits at all four run dates with 200 copies; the current-month gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall.
